title: INCEST, ALCOHOL, AND A CAVE: GENESIS RECORDS WHAT MOST SERMONS AVOID
paragraphs:
INCEST, ALCOHOL, AND A CAVE: GENESIS RECORDS WHAT MOST SERMONS AVOID
Two daughters. One drunken father. Two pregnancies. A family history nobody would want remembered—and generations later, a Moabite woman appears in the family line of Jesus Christ. If you think your past is too stained for redemption, do not look away yet.
There are Bible stories we frame and hang on nursery walls.
Noah’s ark.
David and Goliath.
Daniel among the lions.
Jesus carrying a lamb.
And then there is Genesis 19.
Nobody is embroidering this scene onto a baby blanket.
A frightened father.
Two daughters.
A cave.
Wine.
Incest.
Pregnancy.
And the birth of two nations.
It is one of those passages that can make you wonder why God allowed something so disturbing to remain in Holy Scripture.
Why not leave this part out?
Why preserve something this ugly?
Perhaps because the Bible was never written to protect the reputation of humanity.
It reveals our need for God.
And sometimes Scripture takes us into places so dark that we finally understand what grace actually means.
Genesis 19:30 tells us that Lot left Zoar because he was afraid and went into the mountains with his two daughters. There, the three of them lived in a cave.
Think about what these women had just survived.
Their world had collapsed.
Sodom was gone.
Their home was gone.
Their mother was gone.
Their former life was gone.
And now there was darkness, stone, isolation, fear, and a father who had already demonstrated profoundly compromised judgment.
This does not excuse what happens next.
Trauma can help us understand distorted thinking.
It does not transform sin into righteousness.
The older daughter looks at their situation and reaches a desperate conclusion: their father is old, and they believe there is no man available through whom they can continue the family line.
Then comes the plan.
Wine.
Intoxication.
Sex with their father.
Pregnancy.
The Hebrew of Genesis does not sanitize their intention.
Genesis 19:32 contains the expression:
וּנְחַיֶּה מֵאָבִינוּ זָרַע
unechayyeh me’avinu zeraʿ
In context, the idea is essentially:
“that we may preserve offspring through our father.”
There is calculation in those words.
Not romance.
Not covenant.
Not marriage.
Not God's design for sexuality.
A plan.
They will intoxicate their father until he is unaware of what is happening, and then they will use his body in an attempt to preserve descendants.
Genesis records that on the first night the older daughter lies with him, and Lot does not know when she lies down or when she gets up.
Then they do it again.
The younger daughter goes to him the following night.
Again, wine.
Again, intoxication.
Again, sexual violation.
Again, Scripture says Lot does not know when she lies down or rises.
The Bible reports it.
The Bible does not celebrate it.
That distinction matters.
One of the most dangerous ways to read Scripture is to assume that everything the Bible describes is something the Bible prescribes.
It is not.
Scripture records murder without blessing murder.
It records adultery without approving adultery.
It records betrayal without sanctifying betrayal.
And here it records incest without making incest holy.
God's Word is brutally truthful about what human beings can become when fear, lust, desperation, unbelief, intoxication, selfishness, and broken judgment begin governing their decisions.
And perhaps that is why this ancient cave is more modern than we would like to admit.
Your cave may not look like Lot’s.
Maybe yours has Wi-Fi.
Maybe yours has locked browser history.
Maybe yours is hidden behind a respectable marriage.
Maybe yours wears church clothes on Sunday.
Maybe yours appears successful on Facebook while collapsing privately.
Maybe nobody knows what you drink when everyone has gone to bed.
Nobody knows the messages you delete.
Nobody knows what you watch.
Nobody knows the resentment you rehearse.
Nobody knows what happened in your family.
Nobody knows what happened to you.
Nobody knows what you did afterward.
Nobody knows why certain memories still make you feel dirty.
Nobody knows the secret you are terrified your children might discover.
And you have become very good at living outside the cave while emotionally remaining inside it.
That is why Genesis 19 is uncomfortable.
The Bible keeps turning lights on.
And we keep discovering rooms inside ourselves we hoped God would never enter.
But He already knows.
That should terrify hypocrisy.
And comfort the repentant.
Because the God who knows everything about you is the same God who calls sinners to repentance and offers mercy through Jesus Christ.
Genesis 19:36 gives the consequence without decoration: both daughters become pregnant by their father.
Then the children are named.
The firstborn daughter bears a son named Moab.
The Hebrew name is מוֹאָב — Mo’av.

The exact etymology is discussed, but Genesis deliberately places the name beside the daughters’ repeated language about obtaining offspring “from our father,” me’avinu. The narrative wants you to remember where this child came from.
The younger daughter bears Ben-Ammi:
בֶּן־עַמִּי — Ben-ʿAmmi,
“son of my people” or “son of my kin.”
The scandal becomes genealogical.
The secret gets a name.
And the names become nations.
Moab.
Ammon.
Imagine carrying a family history like that.
Imagine someone asking where your people came from.
Some genealogies contain stories families proudly repeat.
Others contain chapters everyone learns not to mention.
And maybe that is where this story suddenly stops being about people thousands of years ago.
Because some of you know exactly what it means to inherit something you never chose.
Addiction traveled through your family.
Abuse traveled through your family.
Infidelity traveled through your family.
Anger traveled through your family.
Fatherlessness traveled through your family.
Shame traveled through your family.
You were born halfway into a story somebody else had already damaged.
And perhaps you have wondered whether damaged beginnings require damaged endings.
Then the Bible does something breathtaking.
It keeps going.
Genesis is not the end of Moab’s story.
Generations pass.
And eventually Scripture introduces us to a woman named Ruth.
A Moabite.
Let that sit for a moment.
Ruth came from the people whose ancestral story Genesis connects to that cave.
But Scripture does not imprison Ruth inside Genesis 19.
She is not personally guilty for the sins of Lot and his daughters.
She does not have to reenact the moral failures of her ancestors.
And neither do you.
You may inherit consequences.
You may inherit wounds.
You may inherit dysfunctional examples.
You may inherit a family name filled with painful memories.
But before God, you do not have to become the sins committed before you.
Ruth makes one of Scripture’s most beautiful declarations of allegiance. She clings to Naomi and turns toward Naomi’s people and Naomi’s God.
Then God writes something into her story that nobody staring only at Genesis 19 could have predicted.
Ruth meets Boaz.
The outsider finds refuge.
The widow finds a redeemer.
The Moabite woman becomes a wife.
And Ruth 4 tells us that Ruth and Boaz have a son named Obed.
Obed fathers Jesse.
Jesse fathers David.
David.
The king.
Suddenly the road has traveled from a cave soaked in shame to the royal line of Israel.
But God is not finished.
Open the New Testament.
Matthew begins his Gospel with a genealogy.
Many readers rush through genealogies because they seem like lists of difficult names.
Do not rush through this one.
Matthew is introducing the Messiah.
And there, embedded in the genealogy of Jesus Christ, are these words:
“Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth.”
Ruth.
The Moabite.
The woman whose ethnic history reached backward toward a scandalous cave now appears in the genealogy leading to David and, ultimately, to Jesus the Messiah.
Be careful here.
God did not need incest in order to bring Jesus into the world.
The daughters’ sin was not secretly righteousness.
Their evil did not become good because God later brought good into history.
That would twist the message of Scripture.
The glory is greater than that.
God is so sovereign that human evil cannot ultimately overthrow His redemptive purposes.
He does not call darkness light.
He overcomes darkness.
He does not rename sin righteousness.
He calls sinners to repentance and redeems those who turn to Him.
He does not tell us that wounds do not matter.
He shows us that wounds do not have to possess the final word.
And that is where this story reaches for you.
Maybe you have spent years believing that if people knew the whole story, they would never look at you the same way.
Perhaps they would not.
But Jesus already knows the whole story.
The chapters before your conversion.
The night you wish you could erase.
The relationship you destroyed.
The years you wasted.
The addiction you fed.
The compromises you justified.
The people you hurt.
The things done against you that still make you recoil.
The choices you made because you were wounded.
The sins that were entirely yours.
He knows where responsibility belongs.
He knows where you were victimized.
He knows where you became the offender.
He knows the difference.
And the Gospel does not ask you to blur those differences.
It calls you into the light.
There is a difference between shame saying, “Hide because you are hopeless,” and conviction saying, “Come into the light because Christ is merciful.”
Jesus did not go to the cross because our sins were small.
He went because our need was catastrophic.
The cross destroys the fantasy that sin does not matter.
Look at Christ crucified and you see how seriously God takes evil.
But the cross also destroys the lie that the repentant sinner is beyond redemption.
Look again.
There is the Son of God bearing sin.
There is holy blood being shed.
There is justice and mercy meeting.
There is forgiveness purchased at immeasurable cost.
There is Jesus Christ doing what your shame could never do.
Your shame can punish you.
It cannot cleanse you.
Your regret can replay the past.
It cannot rewrite it.
Your secrecy can conceal wounds.
It cannot heal them.
Your good works can impress people.
They cannot purchase reconciliation with God.
But Christ can save.
Christ can forgive.
Christ can cleanse.
Christ can make new.
And this is where some people will misunderstand grace.
Grace is not Jesus helping you hide the cave.
Grace brings you out.
Grace is not permission to keep feeding the addiction.
Grace teaches you to renounce ungodliness.
Grace is not God saying your sexual sin never mattered.
Grace is Christ calling you to repent and then giving the repentant sinner a future no amount of shame could manufacture.
Grace does not say, “Stay exactly as you are.”
Grace says, “Come to Jesus exactly as you are—and do not expect an encounter with the risen Christ to leave you unchanged.”
Maybe that is the word you needed tonight.
You are not required to keep living according to the worst chapter of your family history.
Your father’s sin does not have to become your identity.
Your mother’s wounds do not have to become your destiny.
Your family’s addiction does not have to become your inheritance.
The abuse committed against you does not define your worth.
And the sins you personally committed do not have to remain hidden beneath religious performance.
Bring them to Christ.
Not to vague spirituality.
Not merely to positive thinking.
Not to self-forgiveness as though you were your own judge and savior.
To Jesus.
Repent.
Confess.
Believe the Gospel.
Turn from sin.
Stop defending what God calls evil.
Stop trying to baptize your compromise with excuses.
Stop assuming that because God loves sinners He therefore leaves sinners enslaved to what is destroying them.
Jesus forgives.
And Jesus transforms.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin becomes acceptable.
That sinners can be redeemed.
Perhaps you are reading this while fighting something nobody around you understands.
Then be honest.
You do not have to publish the details of your trauma or private sin. Wisdom still matters. But there is something powerful about refusing to let shame convince you that you must disappear.
Someone reading beneath you may need to discover that Christians are not people without scars.
We are people whose scars no longer have to be our gods.
And please hear this carefully:
If this article made you think of someone, do not merely react to it and keep scrolling.
Send it to them.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because clicking “share” is a substitute for obedience, worship, generosity, evangelism, repentance, or discipleship.
It is not.
Your share may put the Gospel in front of someone who would never walk into a church tomorrow.

If you want your online life to glorify God, then use what He has placed in your hands—including your voice, your reach, your profile, your conversations, your resources, and your influence—to point people toward Christ.
Supporting Gospel-centered work can be one expression of that stewardship.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to produce content people consume for thirty seconds and forget.
We want to build a place where believers can keep growing deeper in Jesus Christ through Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment.
Come to Christ.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A church membership cannot save you.
Christian merchandise cannot save you.
Your family name cannot save you.
Your reputation cannot save you.
Only Jesus saves.
And maybe that is why Genesis did not delete the cave.
Maybe God wanted generations of wounded people to know that the Bible is not frightened by ugly family histories.
Scripture can tell the truth about the cave because redemption does not depend upon pretending the cave never happened.
The Bible can name Moab.
Then later name Ruth.
Then name David.
Then open the New Testament and name Jesus.
Not because every event connecting those names was righteous.
Far from it.
But because sin does not get to write the final chapter of God's redemptive story.
There was a cave.
There was alcohol.
There was incest.
There were consequences.
There was shame.
But history kept moving.
And eventually another dark place entered the story.
Another place associated with death.
Another place where hope appeared finished.
A tomb.
And on the third day, the tomb was empty.
That is Christianity.
We do not worship a God who pretends graves are gardens.
We worship the Christ who walks out of graves.

Not because every sentence needs to be remembered, but because one day shame may start whispering again, and you may need the reminder that God's grace is greater than the chapter you wish had never been written.
And comment something real.
“Jesus forgive me.”
“No more hiding.”
“Pray for me.”
“I’m still fighting.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Whatever is true.
Because perhaps the first crack in the cave wall is simply refusing to pretend there is no cave.
Then bring the rest to Jesus.
The Savior who entered human history through a genealogy containing broken people is not intimidated by the broken history you bring to Him.
And never forget this:
The cave may explain where part of the story came from—but Jesus Christ can determine where your surrendered story goes next.
